She frames the difficulty as drive rather than mood, describing herself as 'stopped,' not sad.
What they want out of support: I want to sit down on a free Saturday and actually paint for a couple of hours, and get my RHIA study moving, instead of ending every weekend with everything exactly where I left it.

Predisposing. Maria grew up in a Bronx apartment where her parents' pride in her was enormous and entirely attached to what she produced — honor roll, scholarships, being pointed to at the Fiesta Hondureña as proof that everything the family had left behind in Honduras had been worth it. Nobody was ever cruel; the bar simply moved every time she reached it, so a 95 earned 'and what happened to the other five,' and by high school she was moving it herself before anyone else could. She held herself to a measure she would never have dreamed of applying to her friends — she genuinely admired a friend's rough sketch and privately filed her own finished work under 'derivative' — and meeting a deadline never once counted as doing well, only as the floor. In that house, praise arrived for finished, visible results; things done quietly, for nobody to see, had no way of counting at all.

Precipitating. Seven months ago, in February, her abuela — her mother's mother, who lived ten blocks away and taught her to make baleadas standing on a kitchen stool — died suddenly of a stroke. Maria booked the flights for the Honduran relatives, cooked for three days for the repertorio, and was back at work the Monday after the novena, and everyone told her she was the strong one. What stopped that month was everything that had been hers alone: the watercolors her grandmother used to look at over her shoulder, the camera walks, the journal whose last entry is dated the week before the stroke, the half-read book on the nightstand, and the RHIA study plan she had promised herself for spring. At this summer's Fiesta Hondureña an aunt asked when she was bringing her photographs back to the community table, and Maria heard herself say she was too busy with work; she let the fall exam registration deadline pass two weeks later, and that was when she started looking for help.

Her coping keeps the verdict private and the evidence accumulating: every packed-away paintbox confirms that nothing she starts comes to anything, every new system postpones the test that would prove it, and the silence means no one is in a position to tell her otherwise. It has kept the problem sealed inside her free time, at the cost of her free time.

How life is going overall. good.

What brings them here now. Maria is a 28-year-old medical records specialist reporting difficulty starting and sustaining tasks that are hers alone — trouble concentrating, organizing her own time, and keeping routines — most visible in her painting, photography, journal, reading, and stalled RHIA study, all effectively stopped since her grandmother's death seven months ago. What they want out of support: I want to sit down on a free Saturday and actually paint for a couple of hours, and get my RHIA study moving, instead of ending every weekend with everything exactly where I left it.

Predisposing. Maria grew up in a Bronx apartment where her parents' pride in her was enormous and entirely attached to what she produced — honor roll, scholarships, being pointed to at the Fiesta Hondureña as proof that everything the family had left behind in Honduras had been worth it. Nobody was ever cruel; the bar simply moved every time she reached it, so a 95 earned 'and what happened to the other five,' and by high school she was moving it herself before anyone else could. She held herself to a measure she would never have dreamed of applying to her friends — she genuinely admired a friend's rough sketch and privately filed her own finished work under 'derivative' — and meeting a deadline never once counted as doing well, only as the floor. In that house, praise arrived for finished, visible results; things done quietly, for nobody to see, had no way of counting at all.

Precipitating. Seven months ago, in February, her abuela — her mother's mother, who lived ten blocks away and taught her to make baleadas standing on a kitchen stool — died suddenly of a stroke. Maria booked the flights for the Honduran relatives, cooked for three days for the repertorio, and was back at work the Monday after the novena, and everyone told her she was the strong one. What stopped that month was everything that had been hers alone: the watercolors her grandmother used to look at over her shoulder, the camera walks, the journal whose last entry is dated the week before the stroke, the half-read book on the nightstand, and the RHIA study plan she had promised herself for spring. At this summer's Fiesta Hondureña an aunt asked when she was bringing her photographs back to the community table, and Maria heard herself say she was too busy with work; she let the fall exam registration deadline pass two weeks later, and that was when she started looking for help.

Perpetuating. Her coping keeps the verdict private and the evidence accumulating: every packed-away paintbox confirms that nothing she starts comes to anything, every new system postpones the test that would prove it, and the silence means no one is in a position to tell her otherwise. It has kept the problem sealed inside her free time, at the cost of her free time.

- overpreparation: In place of starting, she builds systems: a twelve-week color-coded RHIA plan in Notion with a study-hours chart that has logged zero hours in six weeks, a folder of forty saved watercolor tutorials, three productivity apps tried and abandoned. The same instinct earns her salary — the release-of-information checklist her whole department uses is hers — but at home the system has quietly become a substitute for the doing.
- hiding_needs: Her mother is still arranging flowers for the parish memorial mass, and telling her that Maria cannot finish a painting feels like handing her more to carry, so when her sister asks if she is okay the answer is 'busy at work.' The hiking group gets the organized, funny version of her, and nobody has been told anything — a structured program felt safer than saying it out loud to anyone she knows.

Protective. The parts of her life with other people in them have not slipped: she is up at six and on the 2 train, still the person her floor emails when Epic misbehaves, and she has not missed a day of work since February. Sunday dinner at her parents' apartment still happens every week, and she has taken over making the tamales since her grandmother died, which nobody in the family says out loud tastes almost right. Daniela still texts 'Trail?' on Thursday nights and Maria says yes more Saturdays than not, and she still helps cook for the Fiesta Hondureña every summer, where half the parish knows her name in two languages. The week has a shape to it — work, Sunday dinner, the Saturday hike — and being the Honduran daughter who shows up is still a role she can fill without effort.
